title: Minimalist Principles: Simon Winkler talks to Mick Earls of 'Use No Hooks' on Breaking and Entering
summary: Simon Winkler talks to Mick Earls, one of the founding members of the iconic disco punk band "Use No Hooks." "Use No Hooks" were a funky outfit who took pains to avoid commercial success. Earls says the band is a product of its time, its place, cheap inner suburban living, and the ideology of minimalism.
transcript:
In this Breaking and Entering interview, dated 21 March 2020 by Triple R, founding member Mick Earls joined Simon Winkler on the line to discuss Use No Hooks and the newly released collection The Job. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: Thank you so much for joining us, Mick.

Mick: Thanks so much for your interest, Simon.

Simon: It's more than interest, it's bordering on obsession. The Job, just released on Chapter Music, is a comprehensive collection of your work, with recordings from, I suppose, 1979 through to 1984. 'Do the Job' was an underground hit that became a cult classic when it featured on Chapter Music's Can't Stop It! II compilation in 2007. As someone at the heart of it, how does it feel to revisit these songs and the band's story in 2020?

Mick: I would say, Simon, it's totally bewildering. I still struggle to understand why young audiences like this material. I'm certainly flattered by it, as we all are, and it's exciting to be fêted in this way after all this time. The band basically broke up in 1983. Suddenly, as a result of Chapter Music's foresight, I suppose we could say now, in putting that track on the compilation CD, it got into dance clubs. People found things to like about it that we probably weren't aware of at the time. So yes, I can't explain it.

Simon: Use No Hooks was a band in multiple incarnations. There was yourself, Arne Hanna and Steve Bourke, who sadly is no longer with us, but at one point did the ensemble total ten people?

Mick: Yes, in one very short-lived phase. All of this happened more or less through a series of experiments. We were always an exploratory kind of outfit who had more or less decided early on that we would never play the same material twice. We'd make up something new for each gig, and we'd even toyed with changing the band's name at each gig. We had a series of packaging labels, starting with Sample Only and then Use No Hooks. I had others in mind, like Fragile and This Way Up, but we got stuck on Use No Hooks, so it remained. It was only in the final, sixth phase, from which came 'Do the Job', that we had anything like a rehearsed set we'd play consistently at different gigs.

Mick: To briefly trace the story, what made it possible was that in 1979, 1980, I'd rented very cheap premises in Collingwood, at a time when such things were possible. This was down in the old industrial part, and you could play music all day and all night at full volume without bothering neighbours. It became a hangout for musicians and friends. Quite often they'd get involved in jam sessions, and we might ask them to join the band, or they might invite themselves. If somebody left, we didn't have set material, so it wasn't as if we'd lost a bass player and had to get another bass player. We'd take whoever came and work up material for the next gig. That's more or less what made it possible, cheap suburban living. At one stage it grew to ten because people came in and offered themselves. We worked up a very large single work. This was the middle phase of the band. We weren't writing or performing songs as such. These were often long, three- or four-part, thirty-minute pieces. Usually there'd be a groove, or a lot of drone material, overlaid with tape-recorded sound. Some of that earlier material is available with the LP as digital downloads, worth checking out for anyone interested in this band and the unlikely prospect of success that seems to be coming our way thirty-seven years later.

Mick: We were playing on the basis of minimalist principles, using all kinds of sound. We started with surf music, but over time drifted into more dance-oriented soul and funk when we acquired a fabulous bass player called André Schuster. From there we delved into music with a heavy rhythmic focus. We spent a whole year as a four-piece trying to develop grooves that could be sustained indefinitely. We had material cooked up that way. Then Stuart Grant from Primitive Calculators came back from Europe and heard us play. He'd always wanted a disco band, and we were playing disco-based beats with other things overlaid. He approached us with the idea of arranging some lyrics I'd been writing, bringing in a female chorus with Marisa Stirpe, Wendy Morrissey and Denise Grant. He arranged this material for them. I started writing these lyrics, this quasi-rap, which was quite new at the time. It's another improvising instrument in a way.

Simon: 'Do the Job' has a powerful rhythm section, but the lyrics are highly satirical. Could you tell us about the political context and the commentary you were making?

Mick: I decided to write 'Do the Job' when the prime minister at the time, Malcolm Fraser, started something like a propaganda campaign promoting overwork as an economic, even existential, necessity. He had this line, 'Life wasn't meant to be easy', which was laughed at a bit at the time. I decided to write 'Do the Job' as a dance tune, as an answer to that, in the tradition of the twist or the mashed potato, or whatever it was. I strung together common expressions and clichés used in workplaces. All the songs I wrote lyrics for had to do entirely with common and familiar phrases: clichés, buzzwords, jargon, euphemisms and management-speak. I ended up with a suite of songs based on that idea, public discourse, public language you hear every day in the media or coming out of politicians' mouths. That's basically the idea.

Simon: You mentioned the space, time and freedom you had in the Collingwood warehouse. Could you tell us more about the Little Bands movement and your connection with what was happening locally?

Mick: This was an incredible phase in Melbourne music. It was started by people in Primitive Calculators and Whirlywirld, in 1978, I think. They decided to form very small bands that would play only fifteen minutes of material. Usually there were people with no advanced or basic musical expertise. The idea was that anyone could play music. Everyone's got some ability, so you do what you can with what you have. These small bands would form, make up a set, play and dissolve. That'd be the end of it. There was no ambition beyond that. They'd come out of the audience, then go back into the audience, and another band would come up. They might get together for a couple of weeks and make up some material.

Mick: This predated our involvement as Use No Hooks. The first phase of Little Bands was more or less finished by late 1979, I think. A lot of the instigators went overseas. Then we got involved. Our rehearsal space in Collingwood was a hangout, and we had equipment, so some of these bands formed there and used it. Some of us got involved, but we'd often play an unfamiliar instrument so you wouldn't have someone with standout musical ability. We hosted that for a while. I think I used to organise the gigs, for probably six or eight months. Then we removed ourselves because we started doing other things. I think I went to Sydney for a while, and Jim Buck from the Incredibly Strange Creatures took it over. I won't give their full name. They have a very long title. The myth has emerged in recent years that Use No Hooks came out of the Little Bands movement, that we were one of those little bands that went on to other things. That's not the case. We already had a solid musical programme before we got involved with Little Bands, and that continued right through, quite separate from it, even though, confusingly, the names Sample Only and Use No Hooks sometimes appear in lists of little bands. It's all a bit confused, but it doesn't matter so much these days.

Simon: It's nice for the myth-building. You describe a dynamic, fluid movement, with people influencing each other and building a larger music community.

Mick: I suppose I can say, Simon, that all of this happened more or less as if the so-called music industry didn't exist. It was entirely disposable. There was no music product likely to come out of it. This was done purely for the thrill of performance and the involvement of people who'd never thought of themselves playing a musical instrument. Suddenly they found themselves performing in front of an appreciative audience.

Simon: I'm glad we have these recordings to revisit and appreciate. You've nominated another song from The Job, 'In the Clear'. Could you tell us about it?

Mick: 'In the Clear' was once again triggered by a phrase from a politician. This was New South Wales premier Neville Wran, whose nickname was Nifty. It was probably 1982 or so. He was facing serious corruption allegations, and he'd been overseas. When he came back, he was besieged by the media at the airport, asking about the allegations. He said, 'I'm in the clear.' I spun a kind of imaginary story about his character, who was affecting an air of super-confidence that he'd be able to override anything. I made a rap using rhyming patterns that would go on until I ran out of rhyme, then I'd pick another rhyme. It's a very long track, but some of the vocal work by the female chorus is almost dreamlike in its allure towards the middle. I think it perhaps suggests one of the things that makes this music appealing now, the sound of these voices. So that's 'In the Clear'.

Simon: Thank you so much for joining us and talking about The Job and the legacy and creativity of Use No Hooks.

Mick: Very much appreciated, Simon. I hope you continue to enjoy the record for the rest of your days.
